introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geology 2 (0755), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2025. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions. ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS.

You are reminded of the value of clear sketches, even when not specifically demanded by the wording of the question, and of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées d'après les notions classiques du programme de Géologie A Level, sans source consultable. Les valeurs chiffrées sont des ordres de grandeur de cours (formulation « about »). Les faits à relire par un géologue avant mise en avant sont signalés ci-dessous.

Le sujet ne comporte aucune figure imprimée : `figures` est vide dans tous les fichiers. Les schémas demandés ou utiles (« value of clear sketches ») sont décrits dans les corrigés (éléments à dessiner, légende) sans valeurs inventées.

Question 6(b)(ii) : « heterolithic unconformity » n'est pas un terme universel des manuels. Il est interprété comme une discordance entre roches de natures différentes, c'est-à-dire une discordance de socle (nonconformity) où des roches sédimentaires reposent sur des roches ignées ou métamorphiques érodées ; le corrigé le dit explicitement. À faire relire par un géologue.

Question 6(a) : durée de vie des graptolites (Cambrien moyen à Carbonifère inférieur) et tendances évolutives (réduction du nombre de branches, passage du biserié au monoserié, changements de forme des thèques) tirées des manuels ; elles sont données en ordres de grandeur.
Question 6(c) : le sujet demande deux facteurs ; le corrigé en traite exactement deux (teneur en silice, température), sans en ajouter.
Points : 12 + 9 + 4 = 25, conformes au sujet ; la sous-question (a) regroupe (i) et (ii) (12 points imprimés une seule fois) et (b) regroupe (i), (ii) et (iii) (9 points imprimés une seule fois).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Briefly discuss Graptolites under the following headings:

(i) Mode of fossilisation;

(ii) Evolutionary changes.

(12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Graptolites** are **extinct colonial marine animals (class Graptolithina, phylum Hemichordata)**, with a skeleton (the **rhabdosome**) made of an **organic, chitin-like (collagen-like) material called the periderm**, composed of one or more branches (**stipes**) bearing cup-like **thecae** (each housed one zooid) and a starting cone, the **sicula**. Most were **planktonic** (floating), the rest were attached to the sea floor. They lived from the **Cambrian (Middle) to the Carboniferous**, and were most abundant in the **Ordovician and Silurian**.

**(i) Mode of fossilisation.**

- The animals lived in the **upper layers of the open sea** and, when they died, their rhabdosomes **sank to the bottom** in **quiet, deep, poorly oxygenated water** (anoxic conditions) where **mud** was being deposited and **no scavengers or oxygen** existed to destroy the remains.
- The organic skeleton was **buried in the fine mud and flattened by compaction**. The volatile parts escaped, leaving a **thin film of carbon (carbonisation)**, so that the fossil is a **flattened, dark or silvery carbonaceous film** on the **bedding planes of black shales and mudstones** (it looks like a pencil mark or a saw-blade).
- Sometimes the periderm is **replaced by pyrite (pyritisation)** which preserves it in relief, and in limestone or chert they may be preserved in **three dimensions** (they can be freed with acid).
- They are therefore common in **black shale (graptolitic facies)** and give a very good record in these rocks.

**(ii) Evolutionary changes.** The graptolites **evolved rapidly** and changed in a systematic way, which gives **graptolite zones** (biostratigraphic zones, useful for correlating Ordovician and Silurian rocks worldwide):

1. **Reduction in the number of stipes (branches):** from many-branched forms (the **dendroid graptolites**, with many stipes, which were bottom-living, attached) to **eight, then four, then two and finally one stipe** (*Dictyonema* to *Tetragraptus* to *Didymograptus* to *Monograptus*).
2. **Change in the attitude of the stipes:** **pendent (hanging downwards), then horizontal, then reclined, then scandent (upright, directed upward)**, so that the stipes finally fused back to back, giving a **biserial form** (*Diplograptus*), and then to a **uniserial form with a single row of thecae** (*Monograptus*).
3. **Change in the arrangement of the thecae:** from **biserial (two rows of thecae)** to **uniserial (one row)**, and **simple tubular thecae became hooked, curved or lobed (spiny)**, with the development of the nema and virgula (a thin rod).
4. **Change of habit:** a change from **bottom-attached (benthic) dendroids to free-floating (planktonic) graptolites**, which spread widely over the oceans.

The group became extinct in the **early Carboniferous**. Each stage of this evolution marks a **zone fossil** that is **widespread, short-lived and easily identified**.

An **unconformity** is a **buried erosion surface (or a surface of non-deposition)** that separates **younger rocks above from older rocks below**, and represents a **gap in the geological record**. It forms after the older rocks are **uplifted, eroded** and then **covered again by new sediments** (sea-level change or earth movements).

**(i) Parallel unconformity (disconformity).** The **beds above and below the unconformity are parallel** (they have the same dip), but they are **separated by an irregular erosion surface**, which represents a **time gap** (missing strata). It is often hard to recognise: the evidence is a **basal conglomerate or a weathered surface (palaeosol)**, **an irregular surface cutting into the lower beds**, and **missing fossil zones**. *Diagram:* horizontal older beds, a wavy line (the erosion surface) and horizontal younger beds above, with a basal conglomerate along the line.

**(ii) Heterolithic unconformity (nonconformity, unconformity between different rock types).** **Sedimentary rocks lie on an eroded surface of igneous or metamorphic rocks** (for example granite or gneiss), that is, the rocks above and below are **of different kinds (lithology)**. The older **igneous or metamorphic rocks** were **exposed by uplift and long erosion**, and the **younger sediments** (often starting with a **basal conglomerate or breccia** of the underlying rock) were deposited later on the irregular surface. *Diagram:* a mass of granite or foliated gneiss, an irregular erosion surface with a basal conglomerate, and flat-lying sedimentary beds above it.

**(iii) Angular unconformity.** The **younger beds lie at an angle** (usually nearly horizontal) to the **older beds, which are tilted, folded or faulted**. The sequence of events is: **deposition of the older beds, then tilting or folding (earth movements), uplift, erosion to a flat surface, subsidence and deposition of younger beds** on the eroded surface. It shows a **long gap in time and a mountain-building event** between the two sets of beds, with the younger beds often starting with a **basal conglomerate**. It is the easiest type to recognise (for example Hutton's unconformity at Siccar Point in Scotland). *Diagram:* tilted or folded older beds, an erosion surface across their edges, and horizontal younger beds above.

**Note:** in each diagram, label the older and younger rocks, the unconformity surface (basal conglomerate) and the dip of the beds.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) List and explain two factors that control the viscosity of magma.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Viscosity** is the **resistance of a liquid to flow**. A high-viscosity magma is thick and flows slowly; a low-viscosity magma is runny.

**1. Silica content (chemical composition).** The **higher the silica ($\mathrm{SiO_2}$) content, the higher the viscosity**. Silica forms **long chains and networks of linked silicon-oxygen tetrahedra** in the melt (polymerisation) that resist flow, so acid (rhyolitic) magma with 70 per cent or more of silica is **very viscous** (thick, slow-moving, trapping gas and giving explosive eruptions, domes and plugs), while **basaltic (basic) magma with about 50 per cent silica** has few linked chains, so it is **fluid** and flows long distances (shield volcanoes and lava plateaus).

**2. Temperature.** **Viscosity falls when temperature rises**: heat gives the ions more energy to break the bonds and the melt moves easily. A hot basalt lava (1 000 to 1 200 degrees Celsius) is **much more fluid** than a cooler rhyolite lava (about 700 to 850 degrees Celsius); as a lava flow cools its viscosity increases until it stops moving.
